guideTitle: Best Patio Heaters for Screened Porches (2026)
metaTitle: Best Patio Heaters for Screened Porches 2026
metaDescription: Seven electric heaters for screened porches compared by infrared and ceramic design, footprint, weather rating, noise and power draw. No propane fumes indoors.
expertTake: The Haimmy 42 inch infrared tower is the best pick because its long tube warms seated guests from head to waist with nine power levels. The SereneLife 900W is the value pick for a small porch that shares a circuit. Anyone tempted to use a propane tower on a screened porch should skip that idea completely, because screens trap exhaust.
introParagraphs: A screened porch is the trickiest place to heat. The screens block insects but not drafts, the roof is low, and the space is semi-enclosed enough that burning fuel is a real hazard.

That narrows the field to electric heaters, and the question becomes which delivery style suits a draft-prone, low-ceiling room. Footprint, cord reach, noise and the weather rating all matter more here than raw output.

products.name: Haimmy 42 in infrared patio heater, 9 levels, 9 hour timer
products.description:
The Haimmy is a 42 inch infrared tower whose heating tube spans about two-thirds of the height. That long tube warms a seated person from head to waist, which suits porch furniture. It offers nine heat modes from 620W to 1500W, so you can hold a gentle output on a mild night.

Infrared heat does not depend on warming the air, which is a major advantage on a porch where a draft can sweep warm air away. It adds no exhaust and no flame, so it is safe in a semi-enclosed room. A timer from 1 to 9 hours means the heater turns itself off if you head inside.

Against a fan heater it is silent and gives direct warmth. Place it at arm's length from seating and keep it away from the screen and curtains. Wipe the tube housing with a dry cloth once it is cool, and keep the cord short and off the floor path. The nine steps pay off most in shoulder seasons, when a full 1500W blast would be too much for a small porch. A tower this tall can tip if a pet or child leans on it, so a clear corner is better than a walkway.
products.bestFor: Porches with a seating group in front of the heater.
pros: Long tube warms seated guests from head to waist
cons: 1500W cannot heat a large porch in wind

products.name: SereneLife 900W infrared heater, IP65, aluminum reflector
products.description:
The SereneLife uses 900W, which is about 3,070 BTU per hour, with an aluminum reflector and an IP65 rating. IP65 means dust tight and protected against water jets, and ETL certification is named in the listing. On a screened porch where rain blows through the screens, the rating is a practical comfort.

A 900W draw is gentle on a shared circuit, so it can run alongside a ceiling fan and a few lights without tripping a breaker. That is the best reason to pick it on an older house with a limited porch circuit.

It will not heat a large porch. Treat it as a warm spot for one or two chairs. Keep it aimed at the seats and away from the screens. Many owners pair a small heater like this with a lap blanket, which feels warmer than a bigger heater on a windy night. The aluminum frame resists rust where damp air collects around a porch floor, and the remote means you never need to reach it.
products.bestFor: Small porches with a shared circuit.
pros: IP65 resists dust and water jets
900W is easy on a shared circuit
ETL certification named in the listing
cons: Too little heat for large groups
Fewer controls than the nine-level towers

products.name: hykolity 38.5 in 1500W infrared heater, dual tubes, IP44
products.description:
The hykolity stands 38.5 inches tall with dual carbon heating tubes and two heat levels. It has an IP44 rating, a 0 to 24 hour timer and a remote. IP44 resists splashes, which is enough for a roofed porch where rain rarely reaches the floor.

Two levels keep the choice simple: low for a mild evening and high for a cold one. A porch that is roofed and screened does not usually need IP65, so the lower rating is acceptable.

Compared with the Haimmy it has fewer steps but a longer timer. Keep it a few feet from the screen and furniture. Check the cord and plug each season. The timer is the quiet safety feature here, so set it every evening so the heater does not run empty. A dual-tube design also lets one tube stay lit if the other fails, though the listing does not promise that behavior.
products.bestFor: Roofed porches where two levels are enough.

products.name: Dr. Infrared 1500W heater, freestanding, wall or ceiling
products.description:
The Dr. Infrared 1500W offers three mounting modes: freestanding with a weighted wheeled base, wall mounted or ceiling mounted. On a porch with a low roof, mounting on a wall or beam can free the floor. It has three power steps of 900W, 1200W and 1500W with a remote.

Carbon infrared heat warms people directly, which helps in a drafty porch. At 1500W it makes about 5,120 BTU per hour, which is the practical ceiling for a plug-in on a 15A circuit.

Against the Haimmy it has fewer power steps but more ways to place it. If your porch has a rafter or a wall with space, mounting is a clean solution. Keep the cord short and off the walkway. Plan the mounting height before drilling, because a heater too high on a low porch ceiling wastes heat and one too low is uncomfortable. Check the clearance the manual lists for the ceiling above it.
products.bestFor: Porches that need a heater off the floor.
pros: Three power steps with a remote
cons: Fewer steps than the nine-level tower
Needs a safe mounting point if hung

products.name: Buyplus 1500W PTC ceramic outdoor heater, 3 modes, overheat shutoff
products.description:
The Buyplus uses PTC ceramic heating, which warms the air that a fan blows past the element, with three output modes and a self-resetting overheat breaker. A non-slip base steadies it. Ceramic fan heaters warm a small enclosed zone quickly.

On a porch the weakness of a fan heater is that moving air is lost to drafts. It works best in a porch with solid walls on the windy side or storm windows. It is compact, which helps on a tight porch.

Against an infrared tower it heats the air rather than the person, so it feels less direct. It is a decent choice for a closed three-season room. Keep it dry and away from curtains. The self-resetting breaker means it can cycle off and on if the vents are blocked, so keep the grille clear of cushions and throws. Dust in the fan is the usual cause of a burning smell at the start of the season.
products.bestFor: Closed three-season porches with little draft.
cons: Warm air is lost in drafty porches

products.name: Aarcinhke 1500W PTC ceramic heater, 20W/750W/1500W
products.description:
The Aarcinhke is a 1500W PTC ceramic heater with three modes of 20W, 750W and 1500W. The 20W mode is a fan-only setting that moves air without heat. The listing claims coverage of about 160 square feet and an overheat shutoff.

A 750W middle step uses half the power of the top step, which suits a mild evening. A 160 square foot claim is generous for 1500W in a screened porch, so treat it as a ceiling for a closed room.

Against the Buyplus it adds a fan-only mode and a clearer coverage claim. It needs the same protection from wind and rain. Use the fan-only setting on warm evenings so the same machine earns its place in summer. Keep the intake grille clean, because lint and pollen choke ceramic heaters faster than most owners expect.
products.bestFor: Porches that want a fan mode as well as heat.
pros: 20W fan mode for summer air movement
cons: Coverage claim assumes a closed room
Warm air is lost in drafts

products.name: 1500W PTC ceramic outdoor heater, 2 second warm-up, 3 modes
products.description:
This 1500W PTC ceramic unit warms up in about two seconds and offers three output modes, overheat protection and a quiet fan. It is marketed as a garage and greenhouse heater as well as an outdoor patio heater. Quiet operation matters on a porch where you want to hear the evening.

A ceramic unit warms the air, so it fits a closed porch better than an open one. Its small size keeps it unobtrusive.

Against the other ceramic units it is the quieter and simpler pick. Keep it dry and out of the rain, since indoor-style ceramic heaters are not made for direct weather. Pull the plug when a storm blows rain through the screens, and move the unit to a dry corner. A small handle or low profile makes that easy, which is another reason to favor compact units on a porch.
cons: Warms air, so drafts reduce its effect

buyingCriteria.explanation: A screened porch has a roof and screens that trap exhaust, so propane and other fuel heaters are not suitable. Electric heaters add no flame or exhaust. This guide lists only electric models for that reason. Carbon monoxide has no smell, so the rule is about the room, not how the heater feels. Many manuals state outright that fuel-burning heaters are for open, ventilated spaces, and a screened room is not one.

An infrared tower such as the Haimmy warms people directly, which holds up in a draft. A ceramic fan heater such as the Buyplus warms the air and works best in a closed three-season porch. If your porch is breezy, choose infrared. A quick test is to hold a lit candle at the seating spot on a windy evening, and if the flame bends, a ceramic heater will struggle. Infrared keeps working because the heat is aimed, not carried in moving air.

A 1500W heater draws about 12.5 amps at 120V, most of a 15A circuit. The SereneLife at 900W leaves room for a fan and lights on the same circuit. Check what else shares the porch outlet. Many older homes put porch lights, a fan and a speaker on one 15A circuit, so a 1500W heater can trip the breaker the first night. A dedicated outlet is the real fix, and an electrician can often add one for a modest cost.

A porch is small, so a 42 inch tower or a ceramic box needs room. Keep any heater about three feet from furniture, screens and curtains. The Dr. Infrared can mount on a wall to free floor space. Measure the walking path before you place anything, because a porch with a heater in the middle feels crowded. Mark the three foot clearance zone with painter's tape on the first evening.

The SereneLife has IP65, the hykolity IP44 and ceramic units are indoor-style. A roofed porch rarely needs IP65, but blowing rain through the screens can reach the floor. Match the rating to how wet your porch gets. A porch that sees rain across the floor in storms deserves IP65, while a dry porch under a deep roof can use less. Plugs are the weak point, so keep them off the floor and under a cover.

Infrared towers are silent, while ceramic fan heaters produce a fan hum. On a porch where you want to talk or hear nature, that difference matters. A fan hum around 40 to 55 decibels is typical for ceramic heaters and is noticeable on a quiet night. If the porch is for reading or conversation, silent infrared is the better fit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety in a semi-enclosed room
howWeEvaluated.description: We limited the lineup to electric heaters and checked overheat and tip protection. Fuel heaters were excluded because screens trap exhaust. The SereneLife ETL listing and the ceramic units' overheat shutoffs earned credit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Draft tolerance
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored infrared for drafty porches and ceramic for closed ones. A porch with open screens loses moving warm air quickly, so direct radiant heat ranked higher. The ranking would flip for a fully glazed room.

howWeEvaluated.title: Circuit fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared wattage with typical porch circuits. A 900W heater leaves room for a fan and lights, while 1500W takes most of a 15A circuit. Units with several steps earned credit for lowering the load on mild nights.

howWeEvaluated.title: Footprint
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at height, mounting options and base size. The 42 inch Haimmy takes more floor than a wall-mounted Dr. Infrared. Porches are small, so footprint carried real weight in the ranking.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered cords, fans and remotes, which fail first. Ceramic fans collect dust and wear bearings, while infrared elements are simpler. This section reflects the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns.

maintenance.why: A warm plug signals a poor connection or a thin cord. Replace damaged cords and keep the plug off the floor.
Dust and pollen cook on elements and clog fans. Vacuum the grille with the heater unplugged and cool.
Furniture, cushions and throws creep toward heaters over a season. Re-measure the three foot zone each spring.
Batteries fail in cold weather. Replace cells at the start of the season and keep a spare.
Moisture ruins electronics and corrodes plugs. Cover or store the heater indoors if the porch is left open all winter.

faq.q: Can I use a propane heater on a screened porch?
faq.a: No. Screens and a roof trap exhaust, and carbon monoxide has no smell. Choose an electric heater and keep a battery alarm in any enclosed space.
Infrared for drafty porches, ceramic for closed ones. Infrared warms you directly and stays silent, while ceramic warms the air and hums. Pick by how much wind your porch sees.

faq.q: How much power does it use?
faq.a: 1500W uses 1.5 kWh per hour at full power. Lower steps use less, so a 900W or 750W setting suits a mild evening.

faq.q: Do I need a rain rating?
faq.a: IP44 for a roofed porch, IP65 for blowing rain. Neither covers the plug, so keep it dry. Move a ceramic unit indoors if storms blow through the screens.

faq.q: Can I use an extension cord?
faq.a: Only a heavy outdoor cord rated for the load. A thin cord overheats at 1500W, so keep the run short and the plug cool.
About three feet from furniture, screens and curtains. Follow the exact clearances in the manual for your model.
